text: There are n people labeled one to n. There may be a town judge. The judge trusts nobody, everybody else trusts the judge, and exactly one person fits. You're given trust pairs a, b, meaning a trusts b. Return the judge, or negative one.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — if I read trust as a directed graph where an edge from a to b means a trusts b, then the judge is the one person that everyone else points to, and who points to no one. Is that right?

Then in degree terms, the judge has in-degree n minus one — everyone but themselves trusts them — and out-degree zero — they trust nobody. So I don't actually need to build the graph or traverse it; I just need each person's in and out degree. Are there any constraints on the input size?
n up to a thousand, and up to ten to the fourth trust edges.

Let me run through the example. n is three, and trust is one-three and two-three. Person three is trusted by both one and two, so in of three is two, which is n minus one. And three trusts no one, so out of three is zero. That's the judge — answer three.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to take each candidate and scan the whole trust list to confirm everyone trusts them and they trust no one. That's n times m — re-scanning for every candidate. This problem reminds me of a plain degree count on a directed graph, because the answer only depends on in and out degrees. So I just tally them in one pass and then scan once. That's n plus m — no adjacency list, no BFS or DFS.

Here's the plan. One: two counter arrays, in and out, one-indexed and starting at zero. Two: for each pair a, b, bump out of a and in of b. Three: scan one to n and return the first person with out zero and in n minus one. One thing worth flagging — it's n minus one, not n. The judge doesn't trust themselves, so at most n minus one people can trust the judge; writing in equals n would never match. There's a trade-off here. I could fold both into one score array — plus one when trusted, minus one when trusting — and just check score equals n minus one. Same idea, half the space. I'll keep two arrays for clarity. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop over the trust pairs bumps out of a and in of b. A second loop over one to n returns the first person with out zero and in n minus one, and if nobody matches I return negative one. One thing worth flagging — the arrays have size n plus one because people are labeled one to n. Index zero goes unused, which keeps the labels and indices lined up and avoids off-by-one bugs.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. n is three, trust is one-three and two-three, expected three. Persons one and two each trust someone, so their out-degree is one — not the judge. The row that matters is person three: out zero and in two, which equals n minus one, so it returns three. Let's also test with corner cases. Add three-one, so person three now trusts one: out of three becomes one, nobody qualifies, and it returns negative one. And n equals one with no trust returns one, since in and out are both zero, and n minus one is zero.

The time complexity is n plus m — one pass over the m edges to tally, one pass over the n people to check. The space complexity is linear for the two counters, which folds to one array if I use the score trick. In the worst-case scenario, there's no judge and I scan all n people, still linear. Oh, one more thing — there can be at most one judge. If two people both qualified, each would need everyone else to trust them — but then they'd have to trust each other, contradicting out-degree zero. So the first match I find is the unique answer.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reframed it as pure in and out degree and skipped building a graph entirely. You caught the n minus one detail and explained why it can't be n. And you argued the judge is unique from the degrees, and handled the n equals one edge cleanly. Good work.
